header.act: ACT II — THE COUNCILS TAKE POWER
player.speaker: Revolutionary Delegate
line.reaction-briliant.speaker: Marta Reimers
line.reaction-briliant.text: They heard what your column did in Kiel before your train cleared the junction. Men in these yards repeat the fleet's refusal as if they stood on the decks themselves; the garrison has been arguing with itself ever since.
line.reaction-tactical.speaker: Marta Reimers
line.reaction-tactical.text: The casualty lists reached these yards before you did. Men still came to hear the delegate from Kiel—but the officers had time to read the same telegrams, bar the armouries and prepare for your column.
line.reaction-victory.speaker: Marta Reimers
line.reaction-victory.text: Kiel still holds behind you. That is enough to make this room listen when its delegate speaks—though the officers here have not lost their nerve, and they still command the harbour batteries.
line.callback-naval-base.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
line.callback-naval-base.text: Because your column held the Kiel naval base, its crews have been sending us everything they can spare. Half the rifles against this wall came north on their wagons.
line.callback-naval-base-lost.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
line.callback-naval-base-lost.text: You left Kiel with its naval base slipping back into the officers' hands. Whatever remained in those magazines will be issued to the men sent after us.
line.callback-comms.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
line.callback-comms.text: Your telegraph gamble paid for the journey north: our operators knew Wilhelmshaven had risen before the Admiralty did, and your train passed every signal they tried to close.
line.callback-prisoners-freed.speaker: Marta Reimers
line.callback-prisoners-freed.text: The men from the Arrestlokal came on the train behind yours. They have not let anyone forget whose column opened the gate; half the sailors in this room joined after hearing them tell it.
line.callback-prisoners-breakout-partial: The men you pulled through the service gate came north with us. The rest remained behind Souchon's wall. Artelt says the governor may release them; he no longer builds plans on the governor's mercy.
line.callback-prisoners-abandoned.text: The crowd went to the Arrestlokal without us. Steinhäuser's men fired: eight dead, twenty-nine carried away, the cells still locked. I told the families in the telegraph room. The wire worked perfectly, Delegate.
line.parkhaus-scene.speaker: Marta Reimers
line.parkhaus-scene.text: Mind the rifles against the wall; every chair in the Parkhaus is taken. Sailors in oilskins sit beside stokers, clerks and yard delegates. Hear those three telephones? Yesterday the operators carried every order from the admiral. Today they bring each one to the council first.
line.kuhnt-opening.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
line.kuhnt-opening.text: Those crumpled ballots elected the Council of 21. The admiral still has seals and letterhead; we have the gates, crews and telephone exchange. Your work in Kiel bought us this hour. It did not settle who commands the next one.
line.hug-question.speaker: Paul Hug
line.hug-question.text: The harbour officers hesitate. Aurich, Emden and Oldenburg wait to see whether we move. The council has put its columns under you. Send them out now, or make this base impossible to retake first?
line.hug-question.choice.regional-column: Send columns immediately toward Aurich, Emden and Oldenburg. Political momentum will collapse if the uprising remains trapped inside the naval base.
Gain an untested soldiers' detachment and a prestige award, but forgo full core resupply and the entrenched infantry detachment.
line.hug-question.choice.secure-base.tex: Secure the harbour, station, post and armouries first. A council without a defensible base will be dispersed by the first organised loyalist regiment.
line.hug-question.choice.secure-base.hin: Fully resupply every core formation and gain an entrenched infantry detachment, but forgo the soldiers' detachment and prestige award.
line.kuhnt-regional.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
line.kuhnt-regional.text: Agreed. Each column must carry delegates as well as rifles. We are not occupying foreign towns; we are helping their soldiers and workers form councils of their own.
line.hug-regional-objection.speaker: Paul Hug
line.hug-regional-objection.text: And if Oldenburg strikes while our rifles are scattered among three roads? I will carry the council's order, Kuhnt, but do not call speed a substitute for a defensible base. The towns may welcome our delegates; the garrison will count our battalions.
line.hug-consolidate.speaker: Paul Hug
line.hug-consolidate.text: Then make the base secure quickly. The Oldenburg garrison is the greatest remaining obstacle, and delay gives its officers time to isolate the coast.
line.kuhnt-consolidate-objection.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
line.kuhnt-consolidate-objection.text: You will have your secure harbour. Beyond it, workers who rose because Kiel moved first will watch us guard warehouses while they face their officers alone. If their courage cools before our columns arrive, fortifications will not recover it.
line.oldenburg-report.speaker: Marta Reimers
line.oldenburg-report.text: At every station someone ties a red ribbon to my sleeve and asks whose orders you carry. Workers will stop trains; soldiers may listen. The Oldenburg officers are counting the same rifles while we talk.
line.kuhnt-final.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
line.kuhnt-final.text: Then we make the calculation for them. Carry council resolutions with the rifles, disarm officers who organise resistance, and leave elected delegates behind every column. We are not replacing one distant command with another—we are teaching each town to command itself.
